shots.narration: EVE Online slows time in star systems whose servers are overloaded. Pilots in the battle live fewer minutes than everyone else. What if the universe does this too — and we call it gravity?

shots.sub: Experiment 002 · idea credited to Whitworth (2008) & Alagoz (2010) · we built it

shots.text: mass → load → slower ticks → falling → bent light
shots.sub: testing each link with a runnable model
shots.narration: More stuff in a region, more to compute, so that region updates slower. Let's test every link.
One rule per region: match your neighbours' clock rate, minus your own workload.
The lag settles into a 1/r shape — Newton's shape. Honest caveat: any rule like this gives Poisson's equation. A construction, not a discovery.
Remove gravity from the code. The only rule: tick your internal clock at the local rate.
It falls 16.00 units — exactly ½gt². This part is Einstein: things fall toward slower time.
Light bends toward heavy regions too — but lag alone gets exactly half the measured bending. Einstein's 1911 mistake. Space must stretch as well.

shots.text: A CPU and a steel ball of equal mass fall identically
shots.sub: gravity sees mass-energy only (equivalence principle, ~10⁻¹⁵) — why would 'cost' mean energy?
shots.narration: The hardest problem: gravity ignores complexity. If cost is clock ticks — and mass is a clock — cost is energy. Maybe.

shots.sub: ✓ slow clocks near mass · ✓ 1/r shape · ✓ falling · ✗ half the light bending · ? why energy
